title: VPC health hypotheses, triage checklist and Terraform debug notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a compact, hypothesis-driven triage checklist for VPC / on-prem private deployments. It focuses on common install/runtime failures, fast canonical tests to validate hypotheses, Terraform module gotchas we've seen in the field, and an upgrade/rollback checklist for routine releases. This is intentionally lightweight so on-call engineers and solutions engineers can run through it quickly during a customer incident.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to Private control-plane + data-plane deployments (VPC-connected and air-gapped on-prem installs).
- Audience: SREs, deployment engineers, solutions eng, and customer ops teams supporting install or upgrade failures.

Quick health check (first 6 tests, < 10 minutes):
1) Control plane reachability
   - From admin host: curl -v https://<control-plane-host>/healthz (expect 200 / valid JSON)
   - If TLS errors: openssl s_client -connect <control-plane-host>:443 -servername <control-plane-host>
2) TF state and API access
   - terraform state list (ensure backend reachable). If backend errors, try terraform init with -reconfigure.
3) Node readiness and daemon processes
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl get pods -A | egrep "(CrashLoopBackOff|ImagePullBackOff|Error)"
   - journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200 on nodes with failing pods
4) Network and DNS sanity
   - dig +short control-plane.internal.local from nodes; curl service IPs from node namespace
   - Check node route table, VPC security groups / firewall rules for destination ports 443, 22, and custom runtime ports (default 32000-32100)
5) GPU / driver / container runtime check (if applicable)
   - nvidia-smi (or rocm-smi), docker ps, ctr -n k8s.io containers list ; verify container runtime has access to GPUs
6) TLS / KMS / secrets access
   - Test secrets fetch: kubectl exec <pod> -- /bin/sh -c 'cat /etc/redwood/credentials || echo "no-creds"'

Hypothesis matrix (symptoms -> quick test -> likely causes -> first action):
- Symptom: Control plane returns 502 / gateway timeout
  Quick test: curl -v /healthz, check control-plane logs
  Likely causes: upstream orchestration (api-server) crashed; LB health checks failing; MTLS/KMS auth broken
  First action: rotate to fallback control-plane (if configured) or restart control-plane pod; check LB health-check path and security group

- Symptom: terraform apply hangs / state lock persists
  Quick test: terraform force-unlock <LOCK-ID> after verifying no active ops; check backend (S3/GCS) permissions
  Likely causes: interrupted upgrade, backend credentials expiring, concurrent apply from CI
  First action: confirm no active operator, snapshot state, force-unlock, rerun plan

- Symptom: Pods stuck ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull
  Quick test: docker pull <image> from node; check registry creds and proxy settings
  Likely causes: container registry auth expired, corporate proxy blocking, image has been deleted
  First action: refresh registry token; check image tag / digest in TF variables; fallback to cached image in node registry if present

- Symptom: High token latency / degraded throughput (runtime slow)
  Quick test: sample latency metrics from grafana per-model, run a single inference call and tail logs
  Likely causes: kernel/driver mismatch after node upgrade; overheating/thermal throttling; excessive batching misconfig
  First action: isolate node, drain, check dmesg for GPU errors, scale up small pool for immediate relief

- Symptom: Persistent KV cache misses causing cost spikes
  Quick test: check cache hit-rate in console, run repeat prompt patterns and watch for cache fill
  Likely causes: cache persistence not mounted, disk pressure, incorrect cache key hashing after code change
  First action: verify PV mounts, available disk, restart cache processes, check recent PRs affecting cache keys

Detailed triage steps (order matters):
1) Reproduce in narrow scope: pick a single failing request or pod and reproduce locally or from host. Capture request ID and timestamps.
2) Gather logs: control-plane, operator, kubelet, container runtime logs on relevant nodes. Steps:
   - kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> --since=30m
   - journalctl -u kubelet -n 500
   - dmesg | tail -n 200 (look for OOM, GPU driver errors)
3) Check infra-level events: cloud provider control-plane (VPC flow logs, SG changes), on-prem switch logs, or recent change events (Jira/PRs).
4) Validate Terraform drift: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -var-file=secrets.tfvars. If plan shows unexpected changes, capture plan output and narrow to resource IDs.

Terraform module notes (common pitfalls & fast remediations):
- Provider version mismatch: lock provider versions in module-level required_providers. Symptoms: plan differences, provider plugin errors. Fix: pin and run terraform init -upgrade only after validation.
- Remote state permissions: failures to read remote state manifest as 'Error checking state' — ensure IAM role/service account has s3:GetObject/list and dynamodb:Query if using locks.
- Implicit dependencies: missing depends_on between network and k8s resources can cause race during apply. If encountering 409s or not-ready resources, add explicit depends_on for critical resources (LB / target groups).
- Module input drift: customers sometimes override module variables in their root module. Validate terraform.tfvars and environment overrides; run terraform show to inspect current values.
- Provider autoplacement: cloud provider updated default VPC/subnet mapping leading to resources in wrong AZs—validate allocated subnets with describe-subnets (or equivalent).

Upgrade plan checklist (pre-upgrade, canary, full rollout):
Pre-upgrade verification:
- Confirm terraform plan shows only expected changes; run plan with a read-only tag to the customer (if required).
- Snapshot state: make a copy of remote state bucket and lock it.
- Run smoke tests against a staging cluster using same TF module inputs.
Canary rollout:
- Upgrade 1 control-plane replica / 1 data-plane node pool (non-GPU) and run full health suite (20–30 min stability)
- Monitor latency, error rate, and CPU/GPU utilization; hold if SLOs change by > 10%
Full rollout:
- Staggered waves: 10%, 30%, 60%, 100% nodes; monitor and pause on anomalies
Post-upgrade validation:
- Run regression evals (sample prompts), verify cache warming, run E2E token cost smoke tests

Quick rollback steps (if canary fails):
1) Pause Terraform (don't run new applies).
2) Restore remote state snapshot to a new state file and run terraform plan to preview rollback changes.
3) For runtime-level issues, replace problematic container image tag or revert to previous runtime helm chart via helm rollback <release> <revision>.
4) If LB or DNS is implicated, switch traffic to previous control-plane endpoint (use DNS TTL or internal load balancer weights).

Metrics, logs and dashboards to check quickly:
- Grafana: request latency P99/P95, model-inference tokens/sec, batch sizes, queue length per model pool
- Console: route-level error breakdown, token-level cost spikes, KV cache hit rate
- Node metrics: GPU mem utilization, GPU ECC errors, node temperature, disk IO
- Logs: control-plane audit log, operator reconcile logs with request IDs

Escalation path and required artifacts:
- Required when escalating to core serving-runtime team: incident timeline, terraform plan & state snapshot, kube manifests of failing deployments, tarball of logs (control-plane + node(s)), and a sample failing request ID.
- On-call SRE: @sre-oncall (Slack) and ping the runtime-core rotation if drivers or kernel faults are suspected.

Common misconfigurations we've seen in customer installs (and quick fixes):
- VPC SGs missing ephemeral port range -> fix by adding egress rule to 32000-32200/TCP.
- MTLS certs rotated but not reloaded in pods -> kubectl rollout restart daemonset/redwood-proxy
- Shared NFS mounts with root_squash causing cache write failures -> change export options or use PVC with RWX CSI driver.

Runbook snippets (commands to run first):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
- terraform init && terraform plan -out=plan && terraform apply plan
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime -f
- openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> -showcerts

Notes to self / unresolved questions for follow-up:
- Add a small synthetic test that exercises KV caching across restarts so we can catch mount/permission regressions during canary.
- We should bake a terraform preflight check that verifies provider permissions and network routes before any plan runs.
- Consider a lightweight agent customers can run (single binary) that performs this quick health suite and returns a formatted report for support.

Post-incident checklist (after resolution):
- Capture timeline and anchor to commits/TF applies.
- Create a minimal repro and add automated test to our upgrade regression suite.
- If TF root causes: update module README with a short section labeled 'Field Patches' and a suggested mitigation.

Appendix: quick sample outputs to copy into support ticket
- kubectl get nodes -o wide -> (copy table)
- terraform state list -> (copy trimmed list)
- control-plane logs snippet (last 200 lines) -> (attach)

End of doc — use this as the short-form triage checklist during customer incidents. Save an annotated incident copy back into the customer folder under shared_drives/engineering/private-deployments/<customer>-incidents/ after each engagement.
